documents.title: M2023.11.28 Motion to Recommend Adoption of AI Policy
documents.stance_why: The policy says 'instructors have the discretion to set their own policies' and that guidelines go in each syllabus, so the decision rests with instructors. It also sets a university default ('Students are prohibited ... unless given explicit permission'), but the central move is delegation, with the ban as a fallback.
documents.summary: A Faculty Senate committee motion recommending a short university AI policy. Instructors set course AI rules and state them in syllabi; absent explicit permission, generative AI is prohibited on exams and assignments, notable uses must be acknowledged, and misuse is reported to the Office of Student Accountability. The PDF has blank adoption and vote fields, so adoption is unconfirmed.

units.why: The motion's opening clause says the committee was charged to investigate 'impact that recent artificial intelligence tools (i.e. ChatGPT) might have on academic integrity'; it explains why and how the policy came about, so it is a process statement (P84), informs only.
units.anchor: charged with investigating the impact that recent artificial intelligence tools
units.frag_start: The Faculty Senate Academic Policies Committee
units.policy: The Faculty Senate Academic Policies Committee was charged on February 22, 2023 with investigating the impact of recent AI tools such as ChatGPT on academic integrity.

units.why: The second whereas clause names the taskforce that was 'charged with researching this issue, writing a report, and developing a policy on the use of AI'; this describes who drafted the policy, so P84 rather than P80 (no enforcement role).
units.frag_start: The Academic Policies Committee created a taskforce
units.frag_end: policy on the use of AI for the University,
units.policy: The Academic Policies Committee created a taskforce of faculty from several disciplines and ITS, charged with researching the issue, writing a report and developing a university AI policy.

units.why: The third clause states the committee 'reviewed the report and proposed policy' and the draft went to senators for review on October 26, 2023; a consultation step in how the policy was made (P84).
units.anchor: A draft of the proposed policy was sent via email to the faculty senators
units.policy: The committee reviewed the taskforce's report and proposed policy, and a draft was emailed to faculty senators for review on October 26, 2023.

units.why: The resolution says 'The Faculty Senate recommends that the University adopt the following AI policy'; it is a recommendation, not an adopted rule, which sets the policy's status and adoption path. P56 is the nearest type; P84 also fits but is already used for the process clauses.
units.anchor: recommends that the University adopt the following AI policy
units.policy: The Faculty Senate recommends that the University adopt the AI policy that follows.
units.fit_note: The unit only states that this is a Senate recommendation to adopt; it sets no principles or scope, so P56 fits only partly.

units.why: The policy opens by recognizing 'diverse potential benefits and challenges of generative AI across academic areas', a balanced rationale. P87 is nearest because it names benefits, though it also names challenges.
units.anchor: Recognizing both the diverse potential benefits and challenges of generative AI
units.policy: The policy recognizes both the diverse potential benefits and challenges of generative AI across academic areas.
units.fit_note: Names benefits and challenges together without specifying any; P87 captures only the benefits half.

units.why: 'instructors have the discretion to set their own policies for the application of these AI tools in their courses' places the decision with each instructor, so P04, not a university-wide rule.
units.anchor: instructors have the discretion to set their own policies for the application

units.why: 'Such guidelines should be detailed in the course syllabi and clearly conveyed to students' tells instructors to state their AI rules in the syllabus; this is P09, addressed to instructors with 'should'.
units.anchor: Such guidelines should be detailed in the course syllabi and clearly conveyed to students.

units.why: 'instructors should report impermissible use of AI to the Office of Student Accountability' sets a reporting step to a central office, so P81 (formal reporting) rather than P36, which classifies misuse.
units.anchor: instructors should report impermissible use of AI to the Office of Student Accountability.
units.frag_start: As in all instances of academic misconduct,

units.why: 'Students are prohibited from employing generative AI tools to complete exams or assignments ... unless given explicit permission' is a default ban with an explicit-permission exception, which is the fallback rule when the instructor gives no permission (P06). P01 is close, but the 'unless' clause makes the fallback framing the better fit.
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from employing generative AI tools to complete exams or assignments
units.policy: Students are prohibited from employing generative AI tools to complete exams or assignments (including papers, projects, computer programs, oral presentations, or other course requirements), unless given explicit permission from their course instructor.
units.fit_note: Also a default ban on graded work (P01); chosen P06 because permission depends on explicit instructor approval.

units.why: The same sentence names 'exams' among covered work, so generative AI on exams is banned unless the instructor explicitly permits it; I code the exam case separately as P22.
units.policy: Students are prohibited from employing generative AI tools to complete exams, unless given explicit permission from their course instructor.
units.fit_note: The exam ban is conditional on explicit instructor permission, which P22 does not mention.

units.why: 'Unauthorized use of generative AI is treated as use of unauthorized assistance from another individual' classifies misuse under existing integrity rules by analogy to a human helper, which is P36; P45 also applies but the sentence is about the violation category.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of generative AI is treated as use of unauthorized assistance from another individual.
units.frag_start: Unauthorized use of generative AI is treated
units.fit_note: Also treats AI like a human helper (P45); no penalty is stated.

units.why: 'all notable uses of generative AI should be acknowledged by the student in writing or via citation at the time of assignment submission' is a disclosure rule that applies 'Regardless of the course AI policy', so P24.
units.anchor: all notable uses of generative AI should be acknowledged by the student in writing
units.frag_start: Regardless of the course AI policy, all notable
units.policy: Regardless of the course AI policy, all notable uses of generative AI should be acknowledged by the student in writing or via citation at the time of assignment submission.

units.why: 'when unsure, students should err on the side of full disclosure' tells students how to resolve doubt about disclosure. P10 is the nearest type (when unsure); P24 is already used for the main rule.
units.anchor: when unsure, students should err on the side of full disclosure.
units.fit_note: P10 is about asking before use; here the doubt concerns disclosure and the advice is to disclose fully rather than ask.

units.why: 'it is their responsibility to seek clarification from their instructors prior to its use' tells students to ask before using AI when unsure about permissibility, which is exactly P10.
units.anchor: it is their responsibility to seek clarification from their instructors prior to its use.
units.frag_start: If students are unsure of the permissibility
units.policy: If students are unsure of the permissibility of the use of generative AI in a specific course context, it is their responsibility to seek clarification from their instructors prior to its use.

notes: Only one included document, a Senate motion with blank adoption fields. No school, computing or coded course documents.
